Learning Objectives
Determine the incidence and risk factors of epidural, pyogenic, and granulomatous (atypical)
spine infections.
Recognize salient findings on clinical examination, and perform appropriate diagnostic
laboratory tests and imaging studies.
Appropriately triage patients with a spine infection into surgical or nonsurgical treatment
pathways.
Identify postinfectious sequelae that should be longitudinally monitored to ensure
biomechanical and neurologic stability.

A spinal epidural abscess (SEA) is a rare diagnosis (Resource 1).
The incidence if SEA is increasing because of the increased number of invasive procedures, the
increased number of immunocompromised patients, and increased intravenous drug use
(IVDU) in the United States.
The distribution of occurrence of SEA in the cervical, thoracic, and lumbar spine is 15%, 50%,
and 35%, respectively.
Staphylococcus aureus is the most common cause of SEA (more than two-thirds of patients)
Other causative organisms include S epidermidis, Escherichia coli, and Pseudomonas aeruginosa.

Epidemiology/Microbiology
SEA is defined as an intraspinal, extradural collection of infectious material. The epidural
space is a potential site of pathology that exists between the dura mater and the
boundaries of the spinal canal, including epidural fat, ligamentum flavum, medial facets,
and the dorsal border of the vertebral body. Although SEA is a relatively rare entity, the
incidence of SEA is increasing.1 Older studies reported that SEA is observed in
approximately 2 per 10,000 admissions per year;2 however, most researchers expect the
current incidence of SEA is two times higher. The increased number of spine procedures
(surgical and injection-based), increased number of patient comorbidities, and increased
IVDU are thought to contribute to the increased incidence of SEA.
The pathogenesis of SEA is multifactorial. The rich plexus of epidural vessels in the spine
allows for hematogenous inoculation and abscess formation in patients with septicemia.
A corollary to that theory involves the low-flow vascular network of cartilaginous end
plates. This creates an environment for bacterial extravasation and spread to the
avascular, immune-shielded disk space. A third possibility is direct extension into the
epidural space from a deep surgical site infection. SEA commonly occurs in patients in
their thirties to sixties, with a smaller modal peak in pediatric individuals. The gender
distribution of SEA is equal.
The most common location of SEA is the thoracic spine (50%), followed by the lumbar
spine (35%) and the cervical spine (15%). The mean cost of management for SEA in 2015
was more than $150,000. S aureus is the causative organism in as many as two-thirds of

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000055
2/25

patients, with SEA caused by methicillin-resistant S aureus increasing.1 Other causative
organisms include S epidermidis, E coli, and P aeruginosa.
Risk Factors
Risk factors for SEA include increasing age, diabetes mellitus, end-stage renal disease, IVDU,
bacteremia, recent spine-related management, and decreased immunocompetence.

Risk Factors
The risk factors for SEA are myriad, synergistic, and related to the severity of the risk
factor. Risk factors include increasing age, diabetes mellitus, end-stage renal disease,
IVDU, bacteremia, recent spine-related management, and decreased
immunocompetence. Despite these known risk factors, SEA can occur without a known
source, accounting for the relatively high rate of delayed or missed diagnosis.
Clinical Presentation
The most common symptom of SEA is pain in the affected region.
Given the prevalence of musculoskeletal neck/back pain in the general population, diagnosis
of SEA often is delayed or missed.
If the abscess is located at spinal cord level, myelopathic symptoms may occur.
At the level of the cauda equina, symptoms include radiculopathy and neurogenic claudication.

Clinical Presentation
The clinical presentation of patients with SEA is varied and dependent on the location
and extent of the infection (Resource 2). The most common symptom is back or neck
pain. Because of the prevalence of back and neck pain in the general population, pain
often is initially attributed to other, less acute etiologies. Therefore, the rate of delayed
or missed diagnosis of SEA is alarmingly high given its associated morbidity. The
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:39 AM
AAOS | Spinal Infections
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000055
3/25

presence of a new neurologic deficit on physical examination generally prompts cross-
sectional imaging studies that lead to the diagnosis of SEA; therefore, delayed diagnosis
is more common in neurologically intact patients.
The trajectory of SEA depends on the virulence of the causative organism, the
immunocompetence of the host, and the initiation of management. Less virulent
organisms may result in a low-grade infection that evolves slowly, requiring a high
degree of clinical suspicion to initially diagnose. Given the anatomic limitations of the
spinal canal, SEA often is accompanied by neurologic symptoms. In the lumbar spine,
this may result in radiculopathy with accompanied pain, sensory disturbances, and
motor weakness of the affected root. If a lumbar abscess causes more centrally based
stenosis, the resulting symptom may be neurogenic claudication. If critical stenosis
develops, then cauda equina syndrome may occur. Typical signs of lumbar involvement
noted on physical examination include sensory changes, motor weakness, and
depression of spinal reflexes. The presence of upper motor neuron signs in patients with
a known lumbar SEA should indicate the possibility of a noncontiguous abscesses.
In the thoracic and cervical spine, potential neurologic sequelae often are more
catastrophic. SEA in these locations may result in upper and/or lower extremity
weakness, depending on the level involved. The resultant myelopathy from
cervical/thoracic spinal cord compression also may result in balance and gait
disturbances, with dexterity changes and abnormal spinal reflexes consistent with an
upper motor neuron lesion. Neurologic symptoms may arise from direct compression of
the neural elements but also from ischemic insult. The ventral surface of the thoracic
spine is particularly prone given the location of the anterior spinal artery. Therefore,
ventral thoracic SEA should be carefully considered because it is associated with an
increased risk of abrupt neurologic compromise.
Diagnostic Studies
Suspicion of SEA warrants a complete blood count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), and
C-reactive protein (CRP) level along with blood cultures.
SEND FEEDBACK

AAOS | Spinal Infections
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000055
4/25

Plain radiography does not aid in the diagnosis of SEA. MRI is the preferred imaging modality
for the diagnosis of SEA.
SEA discovered in one region of the spine warrants imaging of the remainder of the spine to
rule out noncontiguous abscesses.
CT may aid in understanding the extent of osseous involvement.

Diagnostic Studies
Laboratory data are useful in the diagnosis and management of SEA. An elevated white
blood cell count with a left shift, ESR, and CRP level indicate an infectious process. Blood
culture data can be used to identify a causative pathogen and direct antibiotic therapy.
Culture data often are obtained by outside hospitals before the initiation of antibiotic
agents and transfer to a tertiary center.
MRI should be performed in patients with an infectious process and worsening
back/neck pain or any neurologic symptoms. Plain radiography is not of value and
should not be used in the initial diagnosis of SEA. Often, radiology departments can
sequence screening MRI of the entire spine and focus on concerning lesions if observed.
If a screening MRI of the entire spine is unavailable, the area of focus should be directed
by the patient history and physical examination findings. SEA discovered in one region of
the spine warrants imaging of the remainder of the spine to evaluate for noncontiguous
lesions, which are present in as many as 10% of patients with SEA.3 MRI may aid in
distinguishing an abscess from phlegmon. An active abscess will display rim
enhancement, whereas epidural phlegmon does not enhance with the administration of
gadolinium. Often, distinction between phlegmon and an abscess is difficult because the
pathologies represent a continuum of an infectious process. Regardless, treatment
principles should be dictated by the risk for neurologic progression.
After a SEA is identified on MRI, CT and upright radiography may aid in understanding
the extent of osseous involvement. Increased signal observed within osseous elements
on T2-weighted MRIs or short tau inversion recovery MRIs may represent edema rather
than frank involvement. Therefore, CT can be performed to delineate the amount of
SEND FEEDBACK

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000055
5/25

involvement, and upright radiography can be performed to evaluate biomechanical
instability with physiologic loading.
Management
Goals
The goals in the management of SEA are to eradicate the infection and preserve neurologic
and biomechanical stability.

Goals
The goals in the management of SEA are infection eradication, preservation or
restoration of neurologic function, and maintenance of biomechanical stability.
Historically, SEA was almost uniformly managed surgically. However, recent clinical
research efforts have examined data to determine indications for surgical and
nonsurgical management.
Nonsurgical Management
Nonsurgical treatment may be considered in patients who are neurologically intact.
Speciation of the causative organism should be attempted via blood cultures.
If blood cultures are not informative, then CT-guided aspiration of infected areas outside of
the spinal canal (such as paraspinal abscess or transpedicular bone biopsies if vertebral
osteomyelitis [VOM] is present) can be performed.

Nonsurgical Management
Nonsurgical treatment should be considered in patients who are neurologically intact.
The risk of neurologic progression in patients who undergo nonsurgical treatment is
dependent on bacterial virulence, location of the abscess, and host factors. Successful
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:39 AM
AAOS | Spinal Infections
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000055
6/25

nonsurgical management depends on identification of a causative organism and
initiation of effective antibiotic therapy. If blood culture data are not informative, then
CT-guided aspiration may provide helpful culture data without necessitating surgical
débridement.
In patients in whom nonsurgical treatment is selected, clinicians should frequently
monitor for changes in neurologic examination and response to antibiotic treatment. A
reliable initial examination is essential in patients who undergo nonsurgical treatment
because it will serve as a reference point to determine if conversion to surgical
treatment is necessary. Often, response to management is monitored via serial imaging
studies; however, this is counterproductive from a surgeon perspective. In patients
without a worsening neurologic examination, response to antibiotic therapy should be
monitored via clearance of blood cultures or resolved inflammatory markers.
Surgical Management
Surgical treatment should be reserved for patients with acute neurologic deficits, patients with
a high risk for progression/neurologic compromise, and patients in whom antibiotic therapy
fails.
The definition of high-risk has been the subject of recent research, and clinical prediction tools
have been created (Resource 3).
Increasing age, methicillin-resistant S aureus speciation, and diabetes mellitus are risk factors
for progression.
The surgical approach is dictated by the location of the abscess(es) and whether
biomechanical instability is present.

Surgical Management
Surgical treatment should be reserved for patients with acute neurologic deficits and
patients with a high risk for neurologic progression. Patients at high risk for neurologic
progression include patients with methicillin-resistant S aureus infection, patients with
diabetes mellitus, and patients older than 65 years.4 Advanced statistical methods have
allowed for the creation of clinical algorithms that aid in predicting the risk of SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:39 AM
AAOS | Spinal Infections
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000055
7/25

progression based on initial management (nonsurgical versus surgical).5 The purpose of
rapid management is to prevent additional neurologic deterioration and to potentially
restore lost neurologic function. In patients with a delayed, complete deficit, the role of
surgical treatment is less clear. In these patients, the goal of surgical treatment is
establishing source control rather than returning neurologic function, especially if a
complete deficit has been present for more than 3 days.
In patients who are neurologically intact, surgical treatment may be necessary to clear
infectious material. This most often occurs in patients with persistent septicemia despite
antibiotic therapy. Close communication with an infectious disease team is important to
convey the potential morbidity associated with surgical management, depending on the
location of the lesion.
A dorsally-based abscess should be managed via decompression alone, if possible.
Laminectomies of the lumbar and thoracic spine and laminoforaminotomy of the
cervical spine can be performed without fusion and are associated with a low risk of
subsequent iatrogenic instability. In patients with preexisting instability (via spondylotic
or infectious processes) and patients in whom instability is expected after surgical
decompression, instrumented fusion can be performed to ensure biomechanical
stability. Abscesses that arise from ventral osteomyelitis/discitis may require anterior-
based or circumferential decompression. In the cervical spine, this involves anterior
diskectomy/corpectomy and fusion with or without a posterior-based procedure. Ventral
thoracic lesions can be evacuated via transpedicular or costotransversectomy
approaches to avoid the morbidity associated with a thoracotomy. Similarly, lumbar
ventral lesions can be managed via a transforaminal approach and instrumented
reconstruction.
Postinfectious Sequelae
In patients without neurologic dysfunction, successful management of SEA is not associated
with long-term sequelae.
In patients with SEA and VOM, biomechanical instability may be present, and careful follow-up
via upright plain radiography may be helpful.
SEND FEEDBACK

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000055
8/25


Postinfectious Sequelae
Patients with SEA require long-term antibiotic therapy. Depending on the organism and
its sensitivities, this may include intravenous and/or oral therapy. Lifelong oral antibiotic
suppression may be required in some patients who undergo instrumentation. In the
increasingly specialized medical system, experienced infectious disease physicians who
can interpret necessary data, prescribe effective treatment, and monitor for known
complications are essential.
In patients with SEA that resulted in a spinal cord level neurologic injury, physical
medicine and rehabilitation physicians should be involved early to help coordinate
postoperative, spinal cord injury–specific therapies. If permanent root level deficits result
from SEA, bracing may help improve patient function (eg, ankle-foot orthosis for
footdrop). Referrals to surgeons specializing in tendon/nerve transfers may provide
patients with long-term therapeutic options.
Although SEA often occurs in combination with osteomyelitis/discitis, some
biomechanical sequelae are the direct result of SEA alone. Postinfectious instability is
discussed in the next section on hematogenous spine infections.
Hematogenous Spine Infections (Osteomyelitis/Discitis)
Epidemiology/Microbiology
VOM occurs in a bimodal age distribution and is increasing in incidence (Resource 4).
Hematogenous-based infection of the vertebrae is thought to occur in the low-flow
environment of the cartilaginous endplates, which seeds the immune-shielded disk space
(Resource 5).
S aureus is the primary causative organism, with the rate of gram-negative organisms being
20%.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:39 AM
AAOS | Spinal Infections
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000055
9/25


Epidemiology/Microbiology
This section reviews pyogenic spine infections unrelated to prior invasive spine
procedures. Although this section excludes the management of SEA, substantial overlap
exists because of the concomitant nature of the diagnoses. Pyogenic spine infections
result from hematogenous seeding from distant sites. Pyogenic spine infections include
VOM (spondylodiscitis), isolated discitis, and septic facet arthropathy. VOM is the most
common pyogenic spine infection that occurs without a SEA component.
The incidence of VOM in the United States is approximately 5 per 100,000 admissions
per year.6 This is increasing as a result of the rising number of invasive (non-spine)
procedures performed. VOM occurs in a bimodal age distribution in patients in their
teens to sixties. The ventral portion of the osseous vertebral column (vertebral body) is
more involved than the posterior structures. This likely occurs because of the excellent
blood supply of the vertebral bodies. The microbiology of VOM arising from
hematogenous spread mirrors that of the source; therefore, S aureus is the primary
causative organism in patients with VOM. Gram-negative organisms are observed in
approximately 20% of patients with VOM and likely originate from gastroenteric or
urologic infections.
Risk Factors
Risk factors for VOM include increased age, immunosuppression, diabetes mellitus, IVDU,
prolonged corticosteroid use, and malignancy.
The risk factors for VOM are similar to those for SEA and include increased age,
immunosuppression, diabetes mellitus, IVDU, prolonged corticosteroid use, and malignancy.
Clinical Presentation
The most common symptom of VOM is pain in the affected region.
If substantial deformity has occurred by the time of diagnosis, neurologic compromise also
may be present as a result of pressure on exiting nerve roots, the cauda equina, or the spinal
cord.


Clinical Presentation
The primary symptom of VOM is pain in the affected region. The anatomic distribution of
VOM in the lumbar, thoracic, and cervical spine is approximately 60%, 30%, and 10%,
respectively. Fever is noted in only one-third of patients with VOM.7 Tenderness to
palpation is a nonspecific physical examination finding. In addition, VOM is most often
neurologically at baseline in patients without SEA. Therefore, because the most common
symptom of VOM (back/neck pain) is prevalent in the general population at baseline,
diagnosis of VOM frequently is delayed by weeks or months.
Neurologic deficits in patients who have VOM without SEA may occur with progressive
deformity. As the infection evolves, vertebral collapse in the lumbar spine commonly
results in foraminal stenosis and lumbar radiculopathy. In the thoracic and cervical
spine, myelopathic changes may be noted on patient history and physical examination if
the progressive deformity results in spinal cord compression. However, deformity often
is a late-stage finding in patients with VOM. Therefore, suspicion for VOM must remain
high in patients with a recent or current infection if new or worsening pain is reported.
Diagnostic Studies
VOM may result in an elevated white blood cell count, ESR, and CRP level. The latter two
laboratory values are more sensitive and can be used to monitor management. Blood cultures
may help isolate the causative organism.
Plain radiography does not aid in the diagnosis of VOM. MRI is the preferred imaging modality
for the diagnosis of VOM.
CT may aid in understanding the extent of osseous involvement.
Upright plain radiographs should be obtained at the time of diagnosis to evaluate spinal
alignment. This baseline aids in evaluating for progressive deformity.

Diagnostic Studies

Laboratory studies may provide initial confirmatory data or increase suspicion of VOM. A
white blood cell count routinely is obtained but may be normal in as many as 60% of
patients with VOM. In the early stages of VOM, a patient’s ESR may be normal; however,
an elevated ESR or CRP level is associated with a 95% sensitivity for the detection of
VOM.8 These inflammatory markers are helpful from a diagnostic standpoint and
provide an objective metric for monitoring treatment efficacy. Blood cultures are
important during any infectious workup, especially if VOM is suspected. In a patient who
is hemodynamically stable, every effort should be made to obtain blood cultures before
the initiation of empiric antibiotic agents. If blood (urine/fecal) cultures are inconclusive,
then aspiration of the easiest obtainable source should be performed. If the vertebral
body is the only known area of infection and blood cultures are negative, then
transpedicular biopsy (CT-guided or in the operating room) may elucidate the offending
organism (Figure 1).

MRI is the most sensitive imaging modality for the detection of VOM. MRI findings
depend on the stage of VOM. In early VOM before cortical endplate destruction occurs,
hyperintensity within the vertebral body on T2-weighted MRI may be the only finding.
However, as VOM progresses, endplate destruction leads to a predictable loss of
hypointense signal on T1-weighted MRI. In patients with metastatic disease,
distinguishing between VOM and progression of metastases may be difficult, and
experienced radiologists are a helpful resource. In patients without SEA, paraspinal
involvement and enhancement with the administration of gadolinium may help confirm
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:39 AM
AAOS | Spinal Infections
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000055
13/25

a diagnosis of VOM. Disk space involvement is a major criterion suggestive of an
infectious etiology.
CT may be a helpful adjunct in the diagnosis of VOM. CT scans that reveal vacuum
phenomena within the disk space and sclerotic endplates suggest a low likelihood of an
infectious process if MRI findings are equivocal. Other imaging studies, such as
technetium Tc-99m bone scans and indium In-111–labeled leukocyte scans, are
nonspecific compared with MRI and should be used only if MRI is unavailable or
precluded.
From a diagnostic standpoint, the role of plain radiography in patients with VOM is
limited. However, upright plain radiographs may aid in evaluating the biomechanical
stability of the vertebral column. In patients with advanced VOM, progressive
involvement of weight-bearing structures may lead to deformity that is not apparent
until plain radiographs are assessed. Focal deformities may be better visualized on
radiographs involving the affected segments of the spine, whereas full-length standing
spine radiographs may reveal global sagittal or coronal deformity.
Management
Nonsurgical Management
VOM is primarily managed nonsurgically.
The chief predictor of successful management is speciation of the causative organism(s) and
initiation of directed antibiotic therapy.

Nonsurgical Management
VOM is managed nonsurgically in patients without SEA. In patients with hemodynamic
instability, broad-spectrum parenteral antibiotic agents should be administered
imminently in the intensive care setting because of the high mortality rate associated
with septic shock. After a diagnosis of VOM is established, speciation of the pathogen is
the most crucial next step in successful management of the infection.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:39 AM
AAOS | Spinal Infections
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000055
14/25

If a pathogen is identified, antibiotic management is initiated and is usually continued for
4 to 6 weeks. The efficacy of management should be monitored via trending laboratory
data and clinical evaluations. In patients with a neurologic examination that does not
reveal changes, a high threshold should exist for repeat cross-sectional imaging studies
to assess treatment efficacy. Weeks or months may be necessary before resolution of
infectious etiologies is observed on MRI. The role of the orthopaedic surgeon in the
treatment of patients with VOM is to partner closely with an infectious disease team to
inform initial decision making with regard to surgical versus nonsurgical treatment.
Although the selection and duration of antibiotic therapy are under the purview of
infectious disease physicians, a close working relationship may help prevent
unnecessary subsequent imaging studies.
Little evidence suggests that spinal orthoses aid in deformity prevention in patients
undergoing treatment for VOM. Regardless, a spinal orthosis is commonly prescribed to
control pain and support mobilization. If used, non-custom (off-the-shelf) spinal orthoses
are preferred because of the high cost associated with the procurement of custom
spinal orthoses.
Surgical Management
VOM is managed surgically in patients with an acute neurologic deficit.
If progressive deformity develops in the subacute period during antibiotic management as a
result of the extent of vertebral column involvement, surgical management may help stabilize
the spine and restore age-appropriate alignment targets.

Surgical Management
Surgical management of VOM in patients without SEA is reserved for those with a
neurologic deficit, a progressive deformity, or an infection that fails to respond to
antibiotic therapy. In patients without an epidural abscess, neurologic deficits most often
result from progressive deformity. Most of these infections occur in the ventral portion
of the spinal column; therefore, anterior or combined anterior/posterior approaches are
used for débridement and stabilization, if necessary (Figure 2).

abuse. Sagittal MRI (A) and sagittal CT scan (B) show progressive kyphosis and spinal
cord compression as a result of osteomyelitis at C5 and C6. C, Postoperative lateral
radiograph demonstrates anterior corpectomy in combination with posterior
stabilization. (Reproduced with permission from Daniel Tobert, MD, Boston, MA.)
Thoracic and lumbar lesions often can be managed via a posterior-only approach,
depending on the extent of the defect and the degree of deformity. In the lumbar spine,
psoas abscesses often are present and can be débrided by carefully crossing the
intertransverse membrane with the use of a blunt instrument to break up loculations
without damaging the lumbar plexus. Often, the infectious disease team requests
surgical management for patients with VOM that fails to respond to nonsurgical
management. In these patients, careful scrutiny of the infection is necessary. A loculated
paraspinal abscess may evade parenteral therapies and result in persistent bacteremia.
Drain placement by an interventional radiologist often is successful and avoids the
morbidity associated with surgical management; however, if an intradiscal or
intraosseous abscess is identified, then surgical management is a more viable approach.
Postinfectious Sequelae
The natural history of VOM/discitis is fusion of the involved segments.
In patients without neurologic deficit or progressive deformity, nonsurgical treatment via serial
imaging studies should be attempted for at least 3 months to promote nonsurgical fusion.

Postinfectious Sequelae
The natural history of VOM/discitis is fusion of the involved vertebrae. If the infection is
successfully managed via antibiotic agents and the patient is neurologically intact
without progressive deformity, then nonsurgical treatment via serial upright plain
radiographs is recommended. Serial patient histories and physical examinations also
should be performed because they may reveal impending or evolving neurologic deficits
related to progressive deformity (Figure 3).

Granulomatous Spine Infections
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:39 AM
AAOS | Spinal Infections
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000055
18/25

Epidemiology/Microbiology
Granulomatous, nonpyogenic, or atypical infections of the spine are caused by atypical
bacteria and fungi.
These infections are rare and related to residence or travel to geographic areas in which these
organisms are endemic.
Historically, tuberculosis is the most common atypical spine infection; however, the incidence
of tuberculosis has been decreasing in the United States in the past few decades.
Fungal species include Aspergillus, Blastomyces, Coccidioides, Histoplasma, and Cryptococcus.
Atypical bacterial organisms include Actinomyces and Brucella.

Epidemiology/Microbiology
Granulomatous, nonpyogenic or atypical spine infections are caused by atypical bacteria
and fungi. Despite varied biology, these organisms provoke similar clinical and immune
responses in humans. The incidence of these infections is increasing in certain
geographic areas and decreasing in other geographic areas. A concerted effort to
manage Mycobacterium tuberculosis has led to a decrease in tubercular spondylodiscitis
(Pott disease) in the United States and western Europe; however, the incidence of M
tuberculosis is increasing in areas in which it is endemic, such as the Guizhou province in
southwest China.9
The most common granulomatous spine disease is M tuberculosis. M tuberculosis
manifests as extrapulmonary disease in approximately 15% of patients. The most
common area of osseous involvement is the spine, affecting 5% of patients with M
tuberculosis. The spine is inoculated with M tuberculosis via hematogenous routes;
however, direct extension may occur through visceral lesions.
Fungal species often involved in granulomatous disease include Aspergillus, Blastomyces,
Coccidioides, Histoplasma, and Cryptococcus. Some of these fungal species are associated
with known geographic predilections. For example, Coccidioides (Valley fever) is present
throughout the Western Hemisphere but is most often found in the southwestern
United States. Blastomyces is found around the St. Lawrence and Mississippi river valleys
in North America. Likewise, Histoplasma primarily is found in river valleys in central and
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:39 AM
AAOS | Spinal Infections
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000055
19/25

eastern North America. Awareness of geographic endemism may help spine clinicians
maintain suspicion for these rare infections.
Atypical bacteria, such as Actinomyces and Brucella, may less commonly cause spine
infection. Brucellosis is a zoonotic, gram-positive bacterial infection caused by the
ingestion of undercooked animal products. Treponema pallidum is a spirochete that
uncommonly involves the spine.
Risk Factors
Travel or residence in endemic areas is the most obvious risk factor.
High suspicion for infection in immunosuppressed patients (an increasing cohort in society)
may prevent delayed diagnosis.

Risk Factors
Aside from travel to endemic areas, the most common risk factor for these atypical
infections is immunosuppression.
Clinical Presentation
Granulomatous infections are indolent, and neurologic compromise may occur in patients with
an epidural abscess or as a result of progressive deformity.
These infections often are associated with considerable osseous involvement and
biomechanical instability.

Clinical Presentation
The clinical trajectory of these atypical infections is indolent, and neurologic compromise
is the exception. However, neurologic compromise occurs in 50% of patients who have
an atypical infection with an epidural component.10 The low incidence of these infections

and the insidious progression of symptoms may make diagnosis a challenge. In addition,
these atypical infections are commonly systemic and involve multiple organ systems in
immunocompromised hosts, making the interpretation of a patient’s subjective
symptoms difficult. The thoracic region is most affected, and low-grade pain in the
thoracic area is the most common symptom. Kyphotic deformity often is present at the
time of diagnosis because of the substantial vertebral involvement that may occur by the
time diagnosis is made.
Diagnostic Studies
The insidious inflammatory response results in low elevation of traditional inflammatory
markers compared with pyogenic infection.
MRI is the preferred imaging modality, and involvement of the peridiscal vertebral metaphysis
is frequently observed.

Diagnostic Studies
Common laboratory studies for discerning infection may be normal. A patient’s ESR and
CRP level may only be mildly elevated, highlighting the insidious nature of these atypical
infections. Patients with active or previous exposure to Mycobacterium will have a
positive skin test; however, false-negative M tuberculosis antigen skin tests (purified
protein derivative) are known to occur. In general, diagnostic laboratory studies that are
specific to a certain fungus or atypical bacteria should be ordered under the guidance of
an infectious disease specialist. These laboratory studies may include
respiratory/sputum samples or nucleic amplification assays.
Patients with M tuberculosis commonly undergo serial radiography of the chest. Although
this only involves a portion of the spine, AP and lateral radiographs should be scrutinized
closely for signs of vertebral involvement. MRI is the preferred imaging modality to
evaluate for atypical spine infections. Atypical infections commonly germinate in the
peridiscal metaphysis. The disk spaces usually are preserved in patients with these
atypical infections; however, propagation may occur cephalad and caudal to adjacent
vertebrae below the anterior longitudinal ligament. After identification, CT can be

Management
Nonsurgical Management
Given the rarity of these infections, an infectious disease team should be consulted as soon as
possible to help guide appropriate medical therapy.
Biomechanical instability can be monitored via serial upright radiographs if nonsurgical
management is indicated.

Nonsurgical Management
The foundation of atypical infection management is pharmacotherapy, regardless of
progressive spinal deformity or neurologic compromise. The prompt initiation and
completion of medical management affords the best opportunity for infection
eradication. M tuberculosis often is managed with the use of isoniazid, rifampin,
pyrazinamide, and streptomycin/ethambutol for 9 to 12 months. Regular metabolic
studies and blood counts are necessary to prevent known side effects, such as
hepatotoxicity.
Most fungal infections are managed with the use of ketoconazole or amphotericin B,
which may result in profound adverse effects. An increasing problem in the
management of fungal infections is the emergence of strains resistant to available
therapies.
Surgical Management
Surgical management is commonly required for progressive (kyphotic) deformity.

Surgical Management
Prompt surgical treatment is required in patients with a progressive neurologic deficit.
Because progressive neurologic deficits are uncommon in patients with these indolent
infections, partial or systemic eradication and careful surgical planning are permitted.
Surgical treatment is commonly required for patients with kyphotic deformity, with
anterior stabilization commonly performed to correct or prevent additional kyphosis.
Colonization of the titanium implants commonly used in spine surgery is of low concern
in patients with an atypical infection.
